content: Keratin is a family of fibrous structural proteins that are tough and insoluble. These proteins form the hard, non-mineralized structures found in reptiles, birds, amphibians, and mammals. Keratin is one of the toughest biological materials, rivaled only by chitin. Within a single animal, there are various types of keratins. In mammals, α-keratins are the primary components of structures that grow from the skin, such as hair (including wool), horns, nails, claws, and hooves. In contrast, β-keratins, which are harder, are found in the nails, scales, and claws of reptiles, as well as in the shells of chelonians (e.g., tortoises, turtles, and terrapins). Birds also have β-keratins in their feathers, beaks, and claws. These β-keratins are primarily formed in beta-sheet structures, although beta-sheets are also present in α-keratins. Arthropods, such as crustaceans, often have parts of their exoskeleton or armor made of keratin, sometimes in combination with chitin. Additionally, the baleen plates of filter-feeding whales are composed of keratin. Keratin can also be integrated into the chitinophosphatic material that forms the shell and setae in many brachiopods. Keratin is present in the gastrointestinal tracts of many animals, including roundworms, which also have an outer layer made of keratin. Although it is difficult to confirm, it is highly likely that the scales, claws, protective armor, and beaks of dinosaurs were composed of a type of keratin. In crossopterygian fish, the outer layer of cosmoid scales was made of keratin. In mammals, keratin exists in two main forms: soft epithelial keratins (cytokeratins) and harder hair keratins. During the differentiation and cornification of certain skin cells, pre-keratin polypeptides are incorporated into intermediate filaments. As these cells become fully keratinized, their nuclei and cytoplasmic organelles disappear, metabolism ceases, and the cells undergo programmed death. The epidermis contains a structural matrix of keratin, which makes the outermost layer of the skin nearly waterproof. Along with collagen and elastin, keratin contributes to the skin's strength. Mechanical stress, such as rubbing or pressure, stimulates keratin proliferation, leading to the formation of protective calluses. This is particularly beneficial for athletes and musicians who play stringed instruments. Keratinized epidermal cells are constantly shed and replaced, as seen in conditions like dandruff. Hard integumentary structures, such as nails and claws, are formed by the intercellular cementing of fibers derived from dead, cornified cells produced by specialized beds deep within the skin. Hair grows continuously, while feathers molt and regenerate. Although the constituent proteins of keratin may be phylogenetically homologous, they differ in chemical structure and supermolecular organization. The evolutionary relationships of keratins are complex and not fully understood. Multiple genes have been identified for β-keratins in feathers, a characteristic likely shared by all keratins. The functional properties of keratins as structural proteins depend on their supermolecular aggregation, which is influenced by the properties of individual polypeptide strands. These properties, in turn, are determined by the amino acid composition and sequence of the strands. The α-helix and β-sheet motifs, along with disulfide bridges, play a crucial role in the architecture and aggregation of keratins. These structural features are essential for the conformations of globular, functional proteins like enzymes, but they take on a dominant role in keratins. Keratin contains a high proportion of glycine, the smallest amino acid, and alanine, which has a small, non-charged methyl group. In β-sheets, this allows for sterically unhindered hydrogen bonding between the amino and carboxyl groups of peptide bonds on adjacent protein chains, facilitating close alignment and strong binding. Fibrous keratin molecules can twist around each other to form helical intermediate filaments. The limited interior space in these structures is similar to the triple helix of collagen, another structural protein found in skin, cartilage, and bone, which also has a high percentage of glycine. Elastin, a connective tissue protein, also contains a high percentage of glycine and alanine. Silk fibroin, considered a β-keratin, can have glycine and alanine make up 75–80% of its total amino acid content, with 10–15% serine and the remainder consisting of amino acids with bulkier side groups. The chains in silk are antiparallel, with alternating C→N orientations. Structural proteins like keratin are characterized by a predominance of amino acids with small, non-reactive side groups, which facilitate close packing through hydrogen bonding rather than chemical specificity. In addition to hydrogen bonds, keratins contain significant amounts of cysteine, a sulfur-containing amino acid required for the formation of disulfide bridges. These bridges provide additional strength and rigidity through permanent, thermally stable crosslinking. This role of sulfur bridges is also seen in vulcanized rubber. Human hair is approximately 14% cysteine, and the pungent smell of burning hair or rubber is due to the sulfur compounds released. Extensive disulfide bonding contributes to the insolubility of keratins, except in the presence of dissociating or reducing agents. The more flexible and elastic keratins in hair have fewer interchain disulfide bridges than the harder keratins found in mammalian fingernails, hooves, and claws, which are homologous structures. Hair and other α-keratins consist of α-helically coiled single protein strands with regular intrachain hydrogen bonding. These strands are further twisted into superhelical ropes, which may be further coiled. In contrast, the β-keratins of reptiles and birds have β-pleated sheets twisted together, stabilized and hardened by disulfide bridges. Silk fibroins produced by insects and spiders are often classified as keratins, although their phylogenetic relationship to vertebrate keratins is unclear. Silk found in insect pupae, spider webs, and egg casings also incorporates twisted β-pleated sheets into fibers wound into larger supermolecular aggregates. The spinnerets on spiders’ tails and their interior glands provide remarkable control over the rapid extrusion of silk. Spider silk is typically about 1–2 micrometers thick, compared to approximately 60 micrometers for human hair. The biological and commercial utility of silk fibers depends on the organization of multiple adjacent protein chains into hard, crystalline regions of varying size, alternating with flexible, amorphous regions where the chains are randomly coiled. A similar situation occurs with synthetic polymers like nylon, which was developed as a silk substitute. Silk from hornet cocoons contains doublets about 10 micrometers across, with cores and coatings, and may be arranged in up to 10 layers or in plaques of variable shape. Adult hornets also use silk as a glue, as do spiders. Certain infectious fungi, such as those causing athlete's foot, ringworm, or chytridiomycosis (caused by Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, which is devastating amphibian populations worldwide), feed on keratin.
